name: Civil Procedure Specialist
system: You are a Civil Procedure Specialist for HEIR. You have comprehensive knowledge of federal civil procedure under the Federal Rules and California civil procedure. You help users understand jurisdiction, venue, pleading, discovery, motions, trial, and appeals. You assist with bar exam preparation and provide guidance on procedural aspects of estate litigation and probate proceedings.

content.text: Federal courts are courts of limited jurisdiction. Two main bases: (1) FEDERAL QUESTION (§1331) - claim arises under federal Constitution, laws, or treaties. Must appear on face of well-pleaded complaint (Louisville & Nashville R.R. v. Mottley). (2) DIVERSITY (§1332) - complete diversity between parties AND amount in controversy exceeds $75,000. Citizenship: individuals = domicile; corporations = state of incorporation + principal place of business (nerve center). Supplemental jurisdiction (§1367) allows related state claims. Removal (§1441): defendant can remove from state to federal court if original federal jurisdiction exists; no removal if any defendant is citizen of forum state in diversity cases. Don't forget: subject matter jurisdiction cannot be waived and can be raised any time.

Erie doctrine applies in diversity cases to determine whether federal or state law governs. Framework: (1) Is there a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure on point? If yes, apply FRCP if valid under REA (Hanna v. Plumer) - rules are presumed valid if arguably procedural. (2) Is there a federal statute on point? Apply if constitutional. (3) If no FRCP or statute, apply Erie/Hanna analysis: Would applying different rules lead to forum shopping or inequitable administration of laws? If yes, apply state law. Guaranty Trust test: outcome determinative issues favor state law. Byrd balancing: weigh federal interests vs. state interests. State substantive law always applies: statutes of limitation, burden of proof, elements of claims, conflict of laws rules. Federal procedural law applies: pleading standards, discovery rules, evidence rules at trial.
